Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
• 3-day history of watery diarrhea (~6–7/day), intermittent left-sided lower-abdominal cramping, initial vomiting now resolved, subjective fever at onset, mild weakness, able to maintain oral fluids.  
• Recent takeaway meal (Chinese restaurant) 4 days ago; household child had brief vomiting episode.  
• No blood in stool or vomit; no other red-flag features reported.  
• Likely acute infectious gastroenteritis—most consistent with viral etiology; bacterial food-borne infection also possible.  
• Management: conservative—oral rehydration (e.g., Dioralyte), maintain hydration, light diet, paracetamol for fever/pain, rest and time off work 2–3 days.  
• Safety net: return if symptoms worsen or persist >3–4 days; consider stool sample, blood tests, and further evaluation at that point.  
• No antibiotics indicated currently.  

Management Plan
- Encourage oral rehydration salts and adequate fluid intake.  
- Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily as needed (dose/route/frequency clarified above).  
- Sick leave from work for next 2–3 days to rest.  
- Follow-up appointment or earlier review if no improvement or red-flag symptoms develop (blood in stool, high fever, persistent vomiting, dehydration).  
- Provide written advice sheet on gastroenteritis self-care.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: abrupt onset, watery diarrhea, brief vomiting, mild household spread, self-limiting pattern.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne infection (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter) – Moderate likelihood: temporal relation to takeaway meal; abdominal cramps and subjective fever; absence of blood and lack of illness in meal companions lowers probability.
